title: Machine-readable failures for every client command and a consistent selected project
summary: Every client command failure, including an argument-parse error, must end in a non-zero exit and, in machine-readable mode, exactly one structured report with a false success flag, the command the user asked for and the project in effect; human-readable mode prints the message on the error channel only. The selected project must be passed to the engine by every command that acts on a project and must not be passed by a command that does not, and the reported project must equal the project actually sent.
requirements: A client command that acts on a project always sends the selected project to the engine, and the project reported to the caller is the same one that was sent.
A client command that does not act on a project never sends a project.
Any failed invocation — unknown command, missing required argument, malformed numeric limit, remarks that contain no text — exits with a non-zero code.
In machine-readable mode every failed invocation prints exactly one structured report with a false success flag and a readable message, and nothing else on the standard output stream.

That failure report names the command the user asked for and the project in effect at the time of the invocation, whenever the invocation determines them; a value stays empty only when the invocation itself cannot determine it.
In human-readable mode a failed invocation prints the message on the error stream and no structured report.
No failed invocation ends through an unhandled parser exit or prints a language traceback.
A structured refusal from the engine remains a failure even when the engine itself reports success, and keeps the engine's own error fields.
The successful answer of every command keeps its current shape and content.
acceptance: Asking for machine-readable output with a missing required argument produces one structured object with a false success flag, the requested command, the project in effect, a message, and a non-zero exit code.
Asking for machine-readable output with an unknown command produces the same structured failure with the command the user typed.
A non-numeric limit passed to a command produces the same structured failure instead of a traceback.
In human-readable mode the same failures print the message on the error stream and print no structured object.
Every command that acts on a project sends the selected project to the engine, and the reported project equals the sent one; a command that does not act on a project sends none.
Sending a task back with remarks that carry no text is refused with the same structured failure.
constraints: The client stays a thin wrapper: it never invents engine behaviour and never reads project files itself.
Only the failure report changes; successful answers keep their current shape.
All committed artifacts are in English.
assumptions: The next requirement is the first item of the recorded priority list: the project in all commands together with machine-readable argument errors.
The project in effect for a failed invocation is the project stored in the client session, which is written only after the engine accepted it.
The failure report keeps the field names the client already uses for a failed command, adding only the values that were previously empty.
A command that lists projects is treated as not acting on a project.
